title: Schizophrenia - Clozapine Initiation and Monitoring
scenario: Daniel Murphy, a 28-year-old man with treatment-resistant schizophrenia, has been referred for clozapine initiation after failing trials of risperidone 6mg daily and paliperidone 9mg daily. He has persistent auditory hallucinations telling him neighbours are monitoring him through electrical devices. His last hospital admission was 6 weeks ago for psychotic relapse. He lives with his mother who is his primary carer. Take a focused history and explain clozapine monitoring requirements.
patientInstructions: You are concerned about starting a new medication that requires blood tests. You've heard clozapine can be dangerous and want to understand the monitoring process. Reveal that you smoke 20 cigarettes daily and occasionally use cannabis.
candidateInstructions: Take a focused history from this patient with treatment-resistant schizophrenia and explain clozapine initiation including monitoring requirements, side effects, and the mandatory haematological monitoring program.
markingCriteria: Confirms treatment resistance (2 antipsychotics at adequate dose/duration)
Documents current symptoms (hallucinations, delusions, negative symptoms)
Screens for contraindications (history of agranulocytosis, severe cardiac disease, paralytic ileus)
Explains mandatory FBC monitoring schedule (weekly for 18 weeks, then monthly)
Discusses risk of agranulocytosis (1-2%) and neutrophil monitoring thresholds
Explains other side effects (sedation, hypersalivation, weight gain, constipation, myocarditis)
Documents smoking status (affects clozapine levels - smoking induces CYP1A2)
Obtains consent for clozapine patient monitoring system registration
Explains titration schedule (12.5mg nocte, increase by 25-50mg every 2-3 days)
Arranges baseline investigations (FBC, UEC, LFT, lipids, HbA1c, ECG, troponin)
Discusses lifestyle factors (avoid alcohol, maintain regular sleep)
Plans follow-up and emergency contact procedures
sampleResponse: Mr Murphy has documented treatment resistance with adequate trials of risperidone and paliperidone. Baseline FBC shows WCC 8.2, neutrophils 4.8, suitable for clozapine initiation. Will register with clozapine monitoring system today. Starting dose 12.5mg nocte, titrating slowly to target 300-450mg daily. Weekly FBC monitoring mandatory for first 18 weeks - must not dispense if neutrophils <1.5. Smoking status documented - may need higher doses due to CYP1A2 induction. Emergency plan: if fever or signs of infection, urgent FBC and withhold clozapine until results available.
commonErrors: Failing to confirm treatment resistance criteria
investigations: Troponin and CRP (baseline and weeks 1-4 for myocarditis screening)
managementPlan: Initiate clozapine 12.5mg nocte after baseline investigations normal. Register with mandatory monitoring system. Titrate dose by 25mg every 2-3 days to target 300-450mg daily in divided doses. Weekly FBC for 18 weeks, then fortnightly for 1 year, then monthly ongoing. Monitor for myocarditis weeks 1-4 (troponin, CRP, ECG). Address constipation prophylactically with docusate 100mg BD. Review in 1 week, then fortnightly during titration. PBS code: 2182Q (authority required).

title: Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder - Trauma-Focused CBT
scenario: Sarah Chen, a 35-year-old paramedic, presents 4 months after attending a fatal multi-vehicle accident where she couldn't save a child despite resuscitation attempts. She experiences intrusive memories, nightmares, and avoids driving past the accident site. She hasn't returned to work and her relationship is strained. Her GP started sertraline 50mg daily 6 weeks ago with minimal improvement. Assess her PTSD symptoms and discuss treatment options.
patientInstructions: You're struggling with memories of the accident and feel guilty you couldn't save the child. You wake with nightmares 3-4 times weekly. You've been avoiding work and become irritable with your partner. You tried the medication but don't think it's helping much. You're worried about losing your career.
candidateInstructions: Assess this paramedic presenting with PTSD symptoms following a traumatic workplace incident. Use validated screening tools, assess symptom clusters, and discuss evidence-based treatment options including trauma-focused psychological therapy.
markingCriteria: Screens using PCL-5 or similar validated PTSD tool
Identifies all PTSD symptom clusters (intrusion, avoidance, negative cognitions, arousal)
Assesses functional impairment (work, relationships, daily activities)
Screens for comorbidities (depression, anxiety, substance use)
Evaluates suicide risk using appropriate protocol
Reviews current medication and dosing (sertraline subtherapeutic)
Explains trauma-focused CBT principles and evidence base
Discusses EMDR as alternative psychological treatment
Addresses occupational implications and WorkCover
Provides psychoeducation about PTSD and recovery
Discusses medication optimisation (increase sertraline to 100-200mg)
Arranges appropriate follow-up and safety planning
sampleResponse: PCL-5 score 48 indicates severe PTSD meeting DSM-5 criteria. Experiencing all symptom clusters: intrusive memories daily, nightmares 3-4 times weekly, avoiding accident site and work, negative self-blame, hypervigilance, and irritability. Sertraline 50mg subtherapeutic - recommend increasing to 100mg for 2 weeks then 150mg if tolerated. Referring for trauma-focused CBT (12-16 sessions) which has strongest evidence base. Explained this involves gradual exposure to trauma memories in safe environment. WorkCover claim appropriate for workplace PTSD. Safety plan established, no current suicidal ideation but monitoring mood.
commonErrors: Not using validated PTSD screening tool
Not optimising medication dose before changing
managementPlan: Increase sertraline to 100mg daily for 2 weeks, then 150mg targeting therapeutic dose. Refer for trauma-focused CBT with psychologist experienced in first-responder PTSD (12-16 sessions). Provide information about EMDR as alternative. Lodge WorkCover claim for psychological injury. Sleep hygiene education and consider prazosin 1-2mg nocte for nightmares if persist. Review in 2 weeks to assess medication response. Crisis plan includes Lifeline 13 11 14 and emergency department if acute distress. PBS code sertraline: 8302K.

title: Borderline Personality Disorder - Dialectical Behaviour Therapy
scenario: Emma Thompson, a 23-year-old university student, presents to emergency after superficial self-harm (cutting forearms) following relationship breakdown. She has a 5-year history of unstable relationships, self-harm when distressed, and emotional dysregulation. Previous admissions include 2 overdoses. She's been through multiple therapists but 'none understand her'. Currently on quetiapine 100mg nocte and has tried multiple SSRIs. Assess her presentation and discuss DBT as treatment option.
patientInstructions: You feel empty and abandoned after your boyfriend of 3 months ended the relationship. You cut yourself to 'feel something' and relieve emotional pain. You're frustrated that therapists keep leaving or 'giving up' on you. You oscillate between desperately wanting help and feeling hopeless that nothing will work.
candidateInstructions: Assess this young woman presenting with self-harm in the context of borderline personality disorder. Complete a risk assessment, validate her distress, and discuss dialectical behaviour therapy (DBT) as an evidence-based treatment approach.
markingCriteria: Conducts empathetic, non-judgmental assessment
Completes comprehensive risk assessment (self-harm severity, suicidal intent)
Identifies BPD features (unstable relationships, identity disturbance, emotional dysregulation)
Validates emotional distress without reinforcing maladaptive behaviours
Explains DBT components (individual therapy, skills group, phone coaching, consultation team)
Describes four DBT modules (mindfulness, distress tolerance, emotion regulation, interpersonal effectiveness)
Discusses treatment duration and commitment (typically 12 months)
Addresses previous treatment failures sensitively
Develops immediate safety plan for crisis management
Avoids inappropriate hospitalisation for BPD alone
Provides crisis resources (Lifeline, BPD Foundation Australia)
Arranges appropriate follow-up with DBT-trained therapist
sampleResponse: Assessment confirms BPD features meeting 6/9 DSM-5 criteria including unstable relationships, identity disturbance, self-harm, emotional instability, chronic emptiness, and stress-related dissociation. Current self-harm superficial without suicidal intent - using as emotional regulation strategy. DBT recommended as gold-standard treatment with strong evidence base. Explained 12-month program combining weekly individual therapy, 2.5-hour skills group, and between-session phone coaching. Four modules will teach mindfulness, distress tolerance as alternative to self-harm, emotion regulation, and interpersonal effectiveness. Developed crisis plan using TIPP skills (temperature, intense exercise, paced breathing, paired muscle relaxation). Referral to DBT program with 2-week bridging appointment.
commonErrors: Inappropriate hospitalisation for BPD without acute risk
Failing to explain DBT structure comprehensively
managementPlan: Refer to comprehensive DBT program starting within 2 weeks. Program includes: weekly 1-hour individual therapy, weekly 2.5-hour skills group, 24/7 phone coaching for crisis, and therapist consultation team. Continue quetiapine 100mg nocte for sleep/anxiety. Avoid benzodiazepines due to dependency risk. Crisis plan includes TIPP skills, ice packs as self-harm alternative, and crisis contacts (Lifeline 13 11 14, BPD Foundation 1300 134 237). GP follow-up in 1 week for wound check. Avoid unnecessary hospitalisations which can reinforce maladaptive patterns.

title: Eating Disorder (Anorexia Nervosa) - Medical Complications
scenario: Jessica Williams, a 19-year-old ballet student, is brought by her mother with concern about weight loss. Her BMI has dropped from 20 to 15.8 over 6 months. She restricts intake to <800 calories daily, exercises 3 hours daily, and hasn't menstruated for 4 months. She denies any problem and insists she needs to lose more weight for upcoming auditions. Assess medical risk and discuss need for urgent intervention.
requiredEquipment: Medical Emergency in Eating Disorders guidelines
patientInstructions: You don't believe you have a problem and feel your mother is overreacting. You're terrified of gaining weight and losing ballet opportunities. Minimize your restriction and exercise. You feel dizzy on standing and cold all the time but attribute this to training. Be resistant to medical admission initially.
candidateInstructions: Assess this young woman with severe anorexia nervosa, evaluate medical complications and risk, and discuss the need for medical stabilisation and treatment. Address her lack of insight sensitively while emphasising medical urgency.
markingCriteria: Calculates and documents BMI (15.8 = severe anorexia)
Assesses vital signs including orthostatic changes
Screens for medical complications (cardiac, electrolyte, bone density)
Documents amenorrhoea duration and bone health risk
Evaluates cognitive symptoms (concentration, decision-making)
Uses MARSIPAN or similar medical risk assessment tool
Explains life-threatening complications (arrhythmia, hypoglycaemia)
Discusses refeeding syndrome risk and monitoring
Addresses lack of insight without confrontation
Involves family appropriately in treatment planning
Determines need for medical admission (BMI <16 with complications)
Arranges urgent investigations (ECG, bloods, phosphate)
sampleResponse: BMI 15.8 indicates severe anorexia nervosa with high medical risk. Orthostatic hypotension (BP drop 25mmHg on standing) and bradycardia (HR 45) indicate cardiovascular compromise. Amenorrhoea for 4 months suggests hypothalamic suppression and bone loss risk. MARSIPAN criteria indicate need for medical admission. Urgent bloods required: UEC (hyponatraemia, hypokalaemia risk), phosphate (refeeding syndrome), magnesium, glucose, FBC, LFT. ECG shows QTc 485ms (prolonged). Explained life-threatening arrhythmia risk and need for cardiac monitoring during refeeding. Medical admission essential - will start 1200kcal/day with phosphate supplementation and daily bloods. Psychiatric review for Mental Health Act if refuses (risk to self from mental illness).
investigations: UEC, phosphate, magnesium, calcium (refeeding syndrome risk)
DEXA scan (bone density if amenorrhoea >6 months)
managementPlan: Immediate medical admission for stabilisation given BMI 15.8, orthostatic instability, and QTc prolongation. Start controlled refeeding 1200kcal/day, increase by 200kcal every 2 days. Phosphate supplementation 500mg TDS prophylactically. Cardiac monitoring first 72 hours. Daily bloods (UEC, phosphate, magnesium) for 5 days then alternate days. Bed rest until cardiovascularly stable. Psychiatric review for therapy engagement. Family therapy (FBT-AN) once medically stable. If refuses admission, consider Mental Health Act given life-threatening complications from mental illness. Target weight gain 0.5-1kg weekly as outpatient once stable.

title: Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder in Adults - Stimulant Medication
scenario: Michael O'Brien, a 32-year-old IT consultant, seeks assessment for possible ADHD after his 8-year-old son was recently diagnosed. He describes lifelong difficulties with concentration, losing things, starting multiple projects without finishing, and impulsive job changes. His marriage is strained due to forgetfulness and 'not listening'. He tried online focus supplements without benefit. Assess for adult ADHD and discuss treatment options.
patientInstructions: You've struggled with focus your whole life but thought everyone was the same. Since your son's diagnosis, you recognise similar patterns. You interrupt frequently, fidget during the interview, and go off on tangents. You're desperate for help as your wife threatens divorce over your 'carelessness'. You drink 6-8 coffees daily to 'function'.
candidateInstructions: Assess this man for adult ADHD using validated screening tools and developmental history. Discuss diagnosis if criteria met and explain stimulant medication including benefits, risks, monitoring requirements, and PBS authority process.
markingCriteria: Uses validated ADHD screening tool (ASRS v1.1 or DIVA 2.0)
Obtains developmental history (symptoms before age 12)
Documents functional impairment in multiple domains
Collateral history from partner/family if available
Screens for comorbidities (anxiety, depression, substance use)
Cardiovascular risk assessment before stimulants
Explains stimulant options (dexamphetamine vs methylphenidate)
Discusses non-stimulant alternatives (atomoxetine)
Addresses abuse/diversion potential sensitively
Explains PBS authority requirements and restrictions
Discusses non-pharmacological strategies (CBT, coaching)
Plans baseline investigations and monitoring
sampleResponse: ASRS v1.1 score 52/72 highly suggestive of ADHD. Developmental history confirms symptoms from age 6 (school reports document 'disruptive', 'won't focus'). Meets DSM-5 criteria with 7/9 inattentive and 6/9 hyperactive-impulsive symptoms causing significant functional impairment. Cardiovascular screen negative, BP 125/80, no cardiac history. Recommending dexamphetamine trial starting 5mg BD, increasing weekly by 5mg to max 30mg daily. Explained PBS authority requires specialist diagnosis - will complete today. Baseline ECG normal. Discussed side effects (appetite, sleep, BP), monitoring requirements (BP monthly initially), and secure storage. Concurrent referral for ADHD-focused CBT. Partner psychoeducation important. Review in 2 weeks.
commonErrors: Not confirming childhood onset of symptoms
managementPlan: Confirm ADHD diagnosis (combined type) meeting DSM-5 criteria. Start dexamphetamine 5mg BD after cardiovascular clearance. Weekly review during titration to maximum 30mg daily divided doses. PBS authority prescription (code 9473) requires specialist confirmation. Monitor BP and pulse monthly for 3 months then 3-monthly. Address sleep hygiene (stimulants before 2pm). ADHD coaching referral for organisational strategies. Partner education session about ADHD impact. Smartphone apps for task management. If suboptimal response, consider methylphenidate or atomoxetine. Annual review including substance use screening.

title: Substance-Induced Psychosis - Methamphetamine Use
scenario: Jake Robinson, a 26-year-old construction worker, is brought by police after being found agitated and paranoid at a building site, claiming coworkers planted recording devices in his helmet. He last used 'ice' (methamphetamine) 3 days ago after a 5-day binge. He has tactile hallucinations of bugs under his skin and scratches constantly. This is his third presentation in 6 months. Assess and manage his acute presentation.
patientInstructions: You're convinced coworkers are spying on you and put bugs under your skin. You're agitated and want to leave immediately. You minimise drug use ('just helping me work longer shifts'). You become more paranoid when questioned directly about the surveillance. You haven't slept for 5 days.
candidateInstructions: Assess this man presenting with methamphetamine-induced psychosis. Manage acute agitation, differentiate from primary psychosis, and develop a treatment plan addressing both psychosis and substance use.
markingCriteria: Ensures safety (security, calm environment, escape routes)
De-escalation techniques before medication
Documents psychotic symptoms (paranoid delusions, tactile hallucinations)
Confirms methamphetamine use timeline
Differentiates from primary psychotic disorder
Appropriate sedation if required (oral preferred over IM)
Screens for other substance use (alcohol, cannabis)
Assesses withdrawal risk and timeline
Uses Mental Health Act if required for safety
Provides drug and alcohol service referral
Addresses physical health (dehydration, injury from scratching)
Plans follow-up including psychosocial interventions
sampleResponse: Acute methamphetamine-induced psychosis with paranoid delusions and formication (tactile hallucinations). Last use 3 days ago, symptoms should resolve within 7-10 days with abstinence. De-escalation attempted, agreed to oral diazepam 10mg and olanzapine 10mg. Mental Health Act not required as accepted voluntary treatment. IV fluids for dehydration, wound care for excoriations. Explained difference from schizophrenia - substance-induced with clear temporal relationship. Brief admission for safety and monitoring. ASSIST score indicates high-risk use requiring intervention. Referral to MERIT program (Magistrates Early Referral Into Treatment) and Crystal Clear program. Motivational interviewing commenced. Sleep hygiene critical for recovery. Follow-up with D&A service in 1 week.
commonErrors: Using antipsychotics as first-line over de-escalation
investigations: CT head if head injury suspected
managementPlan: Brief admission for safety and stabilisation. Diazepam 10mg QID PRN for agitation weaning over 3-5 days. Olanzapine 10mg nocte for 5-7 days then cease if psychosis resolving. IV fluids 2L over 4 hours for dehydration. Thiamine 300mg IM (Wernicke's prevention). Wound care for excoriations with chlorhexidine. Sleep pack (eye mask, earplugs). Commence motivational interviewing. ASSIST screening indicates high-risk methamphetamine use. Refer Crystal Clear program and MERIT if court involvement. GP follow-up 3 days post-discharge. Housing support if needed. Naltrexone 50mg daily if alcohol dependence.

title: Postnatal Depression - Screening and Management
scenario: Rebecca Martinez, a 29-year-old teacher, attends her 6-week postnatal check with her first baby. She tearfully reports feeling overwhelmed, inadequate as a mother, and disconnected from her baby. She has difficulty sleeping even when the baby sleeps, poor appetite, and intrusive thoughts about accidentally harming the baby. Her partner is concerned she's 'not herself'. Screen for postnatal depression and develop a management plan.
patientInstructions: You feel like a failure as a mother and everyone would be better off without you. You love your baby but feel no connection and this makes you feel guilty. You have scary thoughts about dropping the baby but would never hurt them intentionally. Breastfeeding is difficult and you feel judged. You haven't told anyone how bad you feel.
candidateInstructions: Screen this woman for postnatal depression using validated tools, assess risk including infanticide risk sensitively, and develop a comprehensive management plan that maintains the mother-infant relationship.
markingCriteria: Uses Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS)
Sensitively explores mood, anxiety, and bonding
Assesses intrusive thoughts versus psychosis
Evaluates risk to self (suicide) and baby (infanticide)
Screens for anxiety disorders (common comorbidity)
Discusses normalising aspects (common, treatable)
Explains safe antidepressant options if breastfeeding
Refers for psychological therapy (CBT or IPT)
Considers mother-baby unit if severe
Involves partner/supports appropriately
Addresses practical supports (sleep, household help)
Plans close follow-up and monitoring
sampleResponse: EPDS score 18/30 indicates probable postnatal depression. Experiencing low mood, anhedonia, guilt about bonding difficulties, and ego-dystonic intrusive thoughts without psychosis. No active suicidal ideation but feelings of worthlessness. Intrusive thoughts are anxiety-based (OCD-type) not psychotic - has no intention to harm baby and seeks reassurance. Commenced sertraline 50mg (safe in breastfeeding), increase to 100mg in 1 week. Urgent referral to perinatal mental health service for psychological therapy. Partner education about supporting without taking over care. Maternal child health nurse increased visits. Sleep strategy with partner doing one night feed with expressed milk. Normalised prevalence (15% of mothers). Review in 1 week, earlier if worsens.
commonErrors: Not using validated postnatal screening tool
managementPlan: Sertraline 50mg daily (compatible with breastfeeding), increase to 100mg after 1 week. Refer perinatal mental health service for CBT/IPT within 2 weeks. Partner attending next appointment for psychoeducation. Maternal child health nurse weekly visits focusing on attachment. Mother's group referral for peer support. Sleep hygiene with partner involvement in night feeds. Address breastfeeding challenges with lactation consultant. Safety plan if intrusive thoughts worsen. GP review weekly initially. Consider mother-baby unit if deteriorates (keeps dyad together). Crisis contacts: PANDA 1300 726 306, Lifeline 13 11 14. PBS code sertraline: 2985L.

title: Serotonin Syndrome - Recognition and Management
scenario: David Kim, a 45-year-old accountant with treatment-resistant depression, presents to emergency with confusion, tremor, and profuse sweating. He was started on phenelzine (MAOI) 30mg daily 3 weeks ago after failing multiple SSRIs. Today he took tramadol 100mg for back pain prescribed by a locum GP. His temperature is 38.9°C, HR 130, BP 170/100. He has hyperreflexia and inducible clonus. Diagnose and manage this emergency presentation.
patientInstructions: You're confused and agitated. You can't understand why you feel so unwell after taking pain medication. You're sweating profusely and feel like your muscles are twitching uncontrollably. You forgot to mention the antidepressant change to the locum GP. Keep asking for water and fan yourself constantly.
candidateInstructions: Assess this patient presenting with likely serotonin syndrome from drug interaction. Apply diagnostic criteria, provide emergency management, and educate about medication interactions to prevent recurrence.
markingCriteria: Recognises serotonin syndrome clinical triad (mental state changes, autonomic instability, neuromuscular abnormalities)
Identifies causative drug interaction (MAOI + tramadol)
Applies Hunter Serotonin Toxicity Criteria
Ceases all serotonergic medications immediately
Initiates supportive care (IV fluids, cooling)
Administers cyproheptadine appropriately (12mg stat then 2mg Q2H)
Arranges ICU admission for severe cases
Monitors for complications (rhabdomyolysis, DIC)
Differentiates from NMS, malignant hyperthermia
Documents medication interaction clearly
Plans medication reconciliation and education
Arranges appropriate follow-up
sampleResponse: Hunter Criteria positive for serotonin syndrome: spontaneous clonus, agitation, tremor, hyperreflexia, temperature >38°C. Caused by MAOI (phenelzine) + tramadol interaction. Ceased both medications immediately. Commenced aggressive cooling (ice packs, fans), IV fluids 2L stat. Cyproheptadine 12mg PO/NG stat, then 2mg Q2H until clinical improvement (max 32mg/24hr). ICU admission for monitoring given severity. Bloods: CK 850 (mild rhabdomyolysis), UEC normal, coags normal. Benzodiazepines PRN for agitation (diazepam 5-10mg IV). Temperature decreased to 37.8°C after 2 hours. Will require 2-week washout before alternative antidepressant. Medication alert added to records. Patient and GP education about MAOI interactions essential.
managementPlan: Confirmed severe serotonin syndrome via Hunter Criteria. Immediate cessation phenelzine and tramadol. ICU admission with continuous monitoring. Aggressive cooling to target <38°C. IV fluids 200mL/hr with urine output monitoring. Cyproheptadine 12mg stat then 2mg Q2H (serotonin antagonist). Diazepam 5mg IV PRN for agitation/muscle rigidity. Monitor CK 6-hourly for rhabdomyolysis. If deteriorates: intubation, paralysis with non-depolarising agent, active cooling. Recovery expected 24-72 hours. Require 14-day washout before new antidepressant. Medication review with pharmacist. Alert bracelet for MAOI. Education about tyramine diet and medication interactions.

title: Lithium Toxicity - Monitoring and Treatment
scenario: Margaret Wilson, a 58-year-old with bipolar disorder stable on lithium 1000mg nocte for 10 years, presents with coarse tremor, ataxia, and confusion developing over 3 days. She recently started hydrochlorothiazide for hypertension and has had gastroenteritis with poor oral intake. Her lithium level is 2.1 mmol/L (therapeutic 0.6-1.0). Assess severity and manage lithium toxicity appropriately.
patientInstructions: You're confused about why you're in hospital. Your hands shake uncontrollably and you're unsteady walking. You've been vomiting for 3 days and your GP started a 'water tablet' last week. You can't remember if you've been taking your medications correctly. You're drowsy but rousable.
candidateInstructions: Assess this patient with lithium toxicity, determine severity and precipitating factors, provide appropriate management including consideration for haemodialysis, and plan prevention strategies.
markingCriteria: Recognises moderate-severe lithium toxicity (level 2.1, neurological symptoms)
Identifies precipitating factors (thiazide diuretic, dehydration)
Assesses severity (neurological, renal, cardiac)
Ceases lithium immediately
Commences IV normal saline hydration
Avoids sodium bicarbonate (increases intracellular lithium)
Considers haemodialysis criteria (level >2.5 or >2.0 with severe symptoms)
Monitors lithium levels 6-hourly
Checks renal function and electrolytes
Arranges ECG (T wave changes, QTc)
Plans lithium restart once cleared
Addresses drug interaction education
sampleResponse: Moderate-severe lithium toxicity (level 2.1 mmol/L) with neurological signs. Precipitated by hydrochlorothiazide (reduces lithium clearance) and dehydration from gastroenteritis. Ceased lithium immediately. IV normal saline 200mL/hr targeting urine output >100mL/hr. Nephrology consulted - haemodialysis indicated given level >2.0 with neurological symptoms. Pre-dialysis bloods: Cr 145 (baseline 85), Na 138, K 3.8. ECG shows T wave flattening. Post-dialysis lithium 0.9, but expect rebound from tissue stores - will need repeat levels 6-hourly for 24 hours. Ceased hydrochlorothiazide permanently - use ACE inhibitor for hypertension. Will restart lithium 500mg nocte once level <0.6, with levels twice weekly initially. Medication education essential.
managementPlan: Severe lithium toxicity requiring haemodialysis. Ceased lithium and hydrochlorothiazide. IV normal saline 200mL/hr with strict fluid balance. Haemodialysis x 4 hours, lithium level post 0.9mmol/L. Monitor for rebound - levels 6-hourly x 24 hours. Cardiac monitoring for arrhythmias. Avoid all nephrotoxic drugs. Once level <0.6mmol/L and clinically improved, restart lithium 500mg nocte (50% previous dose). Check levels twice weekly x 2 weeks, then weekly x 4 weeks. Change antihypertensive to ramipril 5mg daily. Patient education: maintain hydration, avoid NSAIDs, report illness promptly. Consider valproate if recurrent toxicity. Document drug interaction prominently.

title: Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome - Emergency Management
scenario: Thomas Anderson, a 24-year-old with first-episode psychosis, was started on haloperidol 10mg BD three days ago. He presents with high fever (40.2°C), severe muscle rigidity, altered consciousness, and autonomic instability. His CK is 4500 U/L. He's diaphoretic with BP fluctuating between 160/100 and 90/60. Recognise NMS and provide emergency management.
patientInstructions: You're barely conscious and cannot provide coherent history. You're rigid like a board, sweating profusely, and your vital signs are unstable. When asked questions, you're confused and disoriented. Your jaw is clenched (trismus).
candidateInstructions: Recognise neuroleptic malignant syndrome in this young man recently started on antipsychotics. Provide emergency management, differentiate from other conditions, and coordinate ICU care.
markingCriteria: Recognises NMS tetrad (hyperthermia, rigidity, altered mental state, autonomic dysfunction)
Immediately ceases all antipsychotics
Initiates aggressive cooling measures
Administers IV fluids for rhabdomyolysis prevention
Considers dantrolene (1-3mg/kg IV)
Considers bromocriptine (2.5-5mg TDS PO/NG)
Arranges urgent ICU admission
Monitors for complications (rhabdomyolysis, renal failure, DIC)
Differentiates from serotonin syndrome, malignant hyperthermia
Orders appropriate investigations
Plans antipsychotic rechallenge after recovery
Documents clearly for future prescribing
sampleResponse: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome confirmed: hyperthermia (40.2°C), lead-pipe rigidity, altered consciousness, autonomic instability, CK 4500. Immediately ceased haloperidol. ICU admission arranged. Aggressive cooling with ice packs, cooling blanket, fans. IV fluids 250mL/hr with urine alkalinisation (sodium bicarbonate) for rhabdomyolysis. Dantrolene 2mg/kg IV given (140mg for 70kg), repeat Q6H if needed. Bromocriptine 5mg NG TDS commenced as dopamine agonist. Lorazepam 2mg IV for agitation (avoid antipsychotics). Continuous cardiac monitoring, core temperature probe. Bloods Q6H: CK peaked 8,000, Cr 110, K 4.8. Intubated for airway protection. Recovery expected 7-10 days. Will require 2-week washout before cautious rechallenge with low-potency antipsychotic (quetiapine). Permanent alert in medical records.
managementPlan: Confirmed NMS - life-threatening emergency. Ceased haloperidol permanently. ICU admission with intubation for airway protection. Core temperature monitoring with aggressive cooling to <38.5°C. IV fluids 250mL/hr with sodium bicarbonate for urine alkalinisation (pH >7.5). Dantrolene 2mg/kg IV Q6H (muscle relaxant). Bromocriptine 5mg NG TDS (dopamine agonist). Lorazepam 1-2mg IV PRN agitation. Monitor CK Q6H until trending down. Haemodialysis if renal failure develops. DVT prophylaxis with compression devices (not heparin until CK falling). Expected recovery 7-10 days. Rechallenge after 2 weeks with quetiapine 25mg, monitor closely. Avoid high-potency antipsychotics lifetime. Medic-Alert bracelet recommended.
